To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Hox code controls vertebral number by a graded repression of Wnt activity in the presomitic tissue.

(i) the number of vertebra is precisely defined, (ii) Hox genes control the total number of somite by collinear repression of Wnt signaling and (iii) this mechanism brings the RA-producing segmented region in close proximity to the tail bud and thereby accounts for the termination of axis elongation.
Hox genes repress Wnt signaling with increasing strength in the tail bud and that this leads to the progressive slowing down of the elongation process, ultimately terminating axis elongation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a vertebrate body plan.
the development of the vertebrate body.
the molecular and genetic mechanisms that regulate the development of the body plan of the vertebrate embryo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

Hox genes control vertebral patterning, segmentation and body elongation by a collinear repression of Wnt activity, which leads to a progressive reduction in PSM size and ultimately brings the RA-producing tail-bud in close vicinity to terminate segmentation and elongation of the vertebral column.

the expression of posterior Hox paralogs in the tail bud is responsible for the termination of somite formation and axis elongation, which is a result of their collinear repression of the Wnt pathway and Brachyury expression.
Hox gene expression in the posterior PSM leads to the repression of Wnt activity, and that this repression is responsible for the slowing down of body elongation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Hox genes control vertebral patterning by repressing Wnt activity in the tail bud, leading to a reduction of PSM, which in turn leads to the progressive activation of RA signaling and the termination of somitogenesis.
the Hox gene expression pattern in the PSM is not just a simple posterior shift, but that it is a progressive repression of Wnt activity that is responsible for the reduction of the PSM.
we show that the Hox code is not only important for the patterning of the body axis but also for controlling its growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Hox genes control vertebral patterning and body size by repressing Wnt signaling activity in a collinear fashion.
Hox genes control vertebral patterning and the length of the vertebral column through the regulation of Wnt signaling.
Hox genes control vertebral patterning and body elongation by repressing Wnt signalling.
